# Presenting our tentative research question and datasets

France has been seeing protests bloom for the past 3 months, first from high schoolers then students and finally these protests welcomed the gilets jaunes and demands about the cost of living.

Violence has been a central topic for these 3 months as both protesters and police officers have been accused of making excessive use of it. Most demands are vividly criticizing the government and people holding power. More than a million people have been in the streets protesting, some of them asking for a new kind of government. As it doesn't seem to be coming, questions arise on the conditions that make for regime change and for protesters to be listened to.

Seeing the current situation in France and the fact that our master is pretty politicized, we have been wondering about different collective actions and their impact. This question also touches on violence and its impact on the response.To study that, there are multiple ways and variables we could look for and try to analyse.

Limiting our analyis to protests and mass mobilization is a deliberate choice although they are not the only ways to express discontentment. For example, analysing the results of boycott could be interesting, or petitions too. We could try to compare different collective action tools that are possible and that have been studied and/or used in the past. However, with the data we have selected for our analysis, our scope remains limited to protests and demonstrations, and mass mobilization.

Moreover, we also wish to put that in relation to the kind of regime these protests are opposing, are they democracies, autocracies, slipping from one to the other ? Is the regime using violence against the protesters ?

It would be interesting to study and see which regime is more likely to see protests emerge. And how they respond to the demands

Finally, we could study the different end scenarios ad even wonder which protests ended up with a regime change ? And how ?

In this project, we would like to try to answer the question :

**Does mass mobilization lead to political regime changes, and to what extent are these results impacted by the nature of the mobilization (violent or non-violent)?**



Looking for datasets on this topic was interesting and we found that Harvard produced two on the subject, along with pdf files explaining their approach and variables. 

The first on is called **mass mobilization**. In this data set, they focus on mobilization against standing powers, government.That way, they also include the response opposed to these mobilizations.
Here, mass mobilization corresponds to at least 50 persons. They used four major newspapers to base their research and they made the choice to exclude protests stemming from foreign policies or religious community. 

The second Harvard dataset is called **NAVCO,for violent and non violent campaigns and outcome**. This data set offers informations that differ from the mass mobilization set. It specifies more context on the campaign and an array of binary variables. It covers data starting from 1900. And they intend to focus on maximalist campaigns, looking to overthrow governments or expel foreign military,separatism, self determination. 

Then, we're using **ACLED's** (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data) data set which simply measures the number of protests and violent demonstrations per country per year. It is an independent, impartial global monitor that collects, analyses, and maps data on conflict and protest. We use their publically available aggregated data entitles "Number of demonstration events by country by year".

Finally, we have de **Episode of regime transformation** (ERT) data set. This data set identifies episodes of democratization and autocratization in V-Dem datasets. Data ranges from 1990 to 2025, including more than 680 episodes of regime transformations.The data contained in this dataset will be key to determine which countries experienced regime changes and when these changes happened.

# First data Set : Harvard's mass mobilization

This Harvard datasets describes about 15 thousands mass mobilization from all over the world, trying to take into account the number of protesters, their violence, demands and the response they got.

```{r}
#| message: false
mass_mob<-vroom(here("data", "mmALL_073120_csv.csv"))
```

Issues that have arisen : - A lot of missing data N/A - Start and end dates in a relatively complicated way (maybe we'll keep them that way and just add the dd/mm/yyyy version) - Inconsistent counting of protesters : from numbers to 1000s, +50 etc. and a tentative category that is incomplete.

### Description of the dataset

#### Number of observations and variables

```{r}
countries<- dplyr::n_distinct(mass_mob$country)
earliest <- min(mass_mob$year)
latest <-max(mass_mob$year)
```

|                        |                      |
|------------------------|----------------------|
| Number of variables    | `{r} ncol(mass_mob)` |
| Number of observations | `{r} nrow(mass_mob)` |
| Number of countries    | `{r} countries`      |
| Earliest year          | `{r} earliest`       |
| Latest year            | `{r} latest`         |

#### Types of variables

As we can see above, this dataset contains 31 variables. We wont present each and every one of them but only those that seem relevant for our research.

| Variables             | Type                                         |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| id                    | `{r} typeof(mass_mob$id)`                    |
| country               | `{r} typeof(mass_mob$country)`               |
| protestnumber         | `{r} typeof(mass_mob$protestnumber)`         |
| protesterviolence     | `{r} typeof(mass_mob$protestviolence)`       |
| participants_category | `{r} typeof(mass_mob$participants_category)` |
| stateresponse1        | `{r} typeof(mass_mob$stateresponse1)`        |

#### Variable description

| Variables | Description |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| id | Unique protest identifier |
| country | Country of the protest |
| protestnumber | Number of the protest in this year |
| protesterviolence | Whether the movement used violence |
| participants_category | Categories summarizing the magnitude of the movement |
| stateresponse1 | How the governing powers reacted to the protests |

### Creating a clean version

We can create a new dataset trying to go around all the NA cells and non ergonomic sides of the dataset.

We can start by adding a column regrouping the dates' information The goal is to get two additional columns : startdate and enddate.

We can also take of the particpants category because it is unusable and might not be relevant to our research.

The counting in this dataset is far from optimal, and there was also the option that a protest = 0, only reporting that there were no mass mobilization that year in this country.

```{r}
filter(mass_mob, protest==0)|>
  nrow()
```

This is the number of rows where there was no protests in the country. We can take this line off.

```{r}
mm_clean <- mass_mob |>
  filter(protest==1) |>
  mutate(startdate=as.Date(paste(startyear,startmonth, startday, sep="-")),
       enddate=as.Date(paste(endyear, endmonth, endday, sep = "-"))) |>
  select(id, country, ccode, year, region, protestnumber, startyear, startdate, endyear,enddate, protesterviolence, protesterdemand1, stateresponse1)
  
```

### Graphical representations

Let's try to get an idea of the data in this dataframe, although, the qunatity of NA data might interfere.

#### Countries with the most mobilizations

```{r}
mass_mob|>
  summarise(nbprotest=sum(protest), .by = country)|>
  slice_max(nbprotest, n=15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=reorder(country,nbprotest), y=nbprotest))+
  geom_col()+
  coord_flip()+
  labs(x="Number of protests", y="Countries")
```

#### Countries with the least mobilizations

```{r}
mass_mob|>
  summarise(nbprotest=sum(protest), .by = country)|>
  slice_min(nbprotest, n=15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=reorder(country,nbprotest, decreasing=TRUE), y=nbprotest))+
  geom_col()+
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x="Number of protests", y="Countries")
```

#### Countries with most violent protests

```{r}
mass_mob|>
  filter(protesterviolence==1)|>
  summarise(nbprotest=sum(protest), .by = country)|>
  slice_max(nbprotest, n=15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=reorder(country,nbprotest), y=nbprotest))+
  geom_col()+
  coord_flip()+
  labs(x="Number of protests", y="Countries")
```

# Second Dataset : Harvard's non violent and violent campaigns and outcomes (NAVCO)

This datasets describes 622 campaigns and simply look at if they were violent or not, a success or not and finally if they ended with a regime change.

This dataset was available to download in .xlsx format which seemed a bit too complicated to navigate for us, plus we also thought it would be simpler to have all our datasets in the same format.

To convert to .csv we used an online converter (Convertio).

```{r}
#| message: false
navco_df<- vroom(here("data", "NAVCO-1.3-List.csv"))
```

Let's first notice there are only two variables in this dataset that have N/A values, each where they represent less that 1%.

# Third Dataset : ACLED's

This dataset contains information on the number of protests and violent demonstrations per country per year.

This dataset was also available to download as an excel file (.xlsx). Thus, following the same logic as for the NAVCO dataset, we used Convertio to convert it into a .csv file.

```{r}
#| message: false
acled_df<- vroom(here("data", "acled.csv"))
colnames(acled_df)
```

This data is already in a tidy format enabling us to clearly observe the evolution of the amount of demonstrations in each country accross the years.

### Number of observations and variables

```{r}

number_of_countries <- dplyr::n_distinct(acled_df$COUNTRY)
minimum <-  min(acled_df$YEAR)
```

# Fourth Dataset : Episodes of regime transformation

```{r}
#| message: false
ert_df<-vroom(here("data","ert.csv"))
```

In this dataset, many of the N/A values come from follow-up variables ie when there is before a binary variable such as democratization episode (dem_ep) and then if there is, what is its name (dem_ep_id). For obvious reason there isn't going to be a name if there isn't anything. So the value isn't missing, it's nothing.

Instead, we could also separate the dataset in regards to if democratization or autocratization episodes were at play.

```{r}
ert_auto <- ert_df |>
  filter(aut_ep==1) |>
  select(-dem_ep, -dem_ep_id, -dem_ep_start_year, -dem_ep_end_year, -dem_ep_termination, -dem_ep_prch, -dem_ep_ptr, -dem_ep_outcome, -dem_ep_outcome_agg, -dem_ep_censored, -dem_ep_subdep, -dem_pre_ep_year)
```

```{r}
ert_dem <- ert_df |>
  filter(dem_ep==1) |>
  select(-aut_ep, -aut_ep_id, -aut_ep_start_year,-aut_ep_end_year,-aut_pre_ep_year, -aut_ep_termination, -aut_ep_prch, -aut_ep_pbr, -aut_ep_outcome, -aut_ep_outcome_agg, -aut_ep_censored, -aut_ep_subreg)

```

## Dataset and variable description

The ert_df dataset identifies episodes of democratization and autocratization in V-Dem datasets. Data ranges from 1990 to 2025, including more than 680 episodes of regime transformations.The data contained in this dataset will be key to determine which countries experienced regime changes and when these changes happened. With the ultimate objective being to determine whether mass mobilization leads to political regime changes, we select a series of variables from this dataset which will be useful for our analysis:

| Variables | Description | Type |
|----------------------|-------------------------|-------------------------|
| country_id | V-Dem country identifier. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$country_id)` (integer, \[3,236\]) |
| country_text_id | V-Dem country identifier in text. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$country_text_id)` |
| country_name | Full V-Dem country name. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$country_names)` |
| year | Year of observation. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$year)` (integer, \[1900,2025\]) |
| v2x_regime | The regime type for the country-year according to Regimes of the World (4 values). | `{r} typeof(ert_df$v2x_regime)` (0 - closed autocracy, 1 - electoral autocracy, 2 - electoral democracy, 3 - liberal democracy) |
| reg_type | Classifies whether the regime in that country-year is a democracy or autocracy. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$reg_type)` (0 - autocracy, 1 - democracy) |
| v2x_polyarchy | Gives the country's score on the Electoral Democracy Index (EDI, V-DEM) in that year. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$v2x_polyarchy)` (interval \[0,1\]) |
| row_regch_event | Measures whether there was a regime change in that country-year according to Regimes of the World (not necessarily "genuine" = followed by elections) | `{r} typeof(ert_df$row_regch_event)` (-1 - change from democracy to autocracy, 0 - no regime change, 1 - change from autocracy to democracy) |
| reg_trans | Measures whether there was a "genuine" regime change in that country-year. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$reg_trans)` (-1 - democratic breakdown, 0 - no regime, 1 - democratic transition) |
| reg_start_year, | Determines the year a regime was founded (needed for the reg_type). | `{r} typeof(ert_df$reg_start_year)` (year, \[1900,2025\]) |
| dem_ep | Whether there is an ongoing democratic episode during the year in that country. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$dem_ep)` (dummy \[0,1\]) |
| dem_ep_start_year | Determines the year the democratic episode began. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$dem_ep_start_year)` (year, \[1901,2025\]) |
| aut_ep | Whether there is an ongoing autocratization episode during the year in that country. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$aut_ep)`(dummy \[0,1\]) |
| aut_ep_start_year | Determines the year the autocratization episode began. | `{r} typeof(ert_df$aut_ep_start_year)` (year, \[1905,2025\]) |

## Cleaning the dataset and variable modification:

The rest of the variables contained in the dataset are removed. This includes: episode description variables and outcome variables, the new dataset is called ert_df_clean:

```{r}
ert_df_clean <- ert_df |>
  select(country_id, country_text_id, country_name, year,v2x_regime, reg_type, v2x_polyarchy, row_regch_event, reg_trans, reg_start_year, dem_ep, dem_ep_start_year, aut_ep, aut_ep_start_year) 
```

Note that the large portion of NA for the dem_ep_start_year and aut_ep_start_year indicate "non applicable" observations, i.e. that there is no episode associated with this particular observation.

Further, as our goal is to determine whether mass mobilization leads to changes in political regimes. Thus, we must modify the dem_ep and aut_ep variables so that they indicate the year the democratization or autocratization episode begins, as opposed to every year it lasts. These variables are particularly interesting for out analysis as they capture the movements towards or away from democratization/autocratization, without necessarily implying a regime switch (which are more rare).

```{r}
ert_df_clean <- ert_df_clean |>
  mutate(
    dem_ep_new = dem_ep == 1 & year == dem_ep_start_year,
    aut_ep_new = aut_ep == 1 & year == aut_ep_start_year
  )
```

## Clean dataset characteristics

Our modified dataset has the following characteristics:

```{r}
number_of_countries <- dplyr::n_distinct(ert_df_clean$country_id)
minimum_yr_ert <-  min(ert_df_clean$year)
maximum_yr_ert <-  max(ert_df_clean$year)
```

|                        |                           |
|------------------------|---------------------------|
| Number of variables    | `{r} ncol(ert_df_clean)`  |
| Number of observations | `{r} nrow(ert_df_clean)`  |
| Number of countries    | `{r} number_of_countries` |
| Earliest year          | `{r} minimum_yr_ert`      |
| Latest year            | `{r} maximum_yr_ert`      |

Given that our goal is to merge our four datasets into one general database, our datasets have to cover the same timespan. The dataset which starts the latest is the ACLED dataset (acled_df) which begins in 1997. The dataset which finishes the earliest is NAVCO dataset (navco_df) which finishes in 2019. Thus our time frame of analysis is 1997-2019. Thus, I further restrict my database:

```{r}
ert_df_clean <- ert_df_clean |>
  filter(year >= 1997, year <= 2019)
```


Our new number of observations is: 

|                        |                           |
|------------------------|---------------------------|
| Number of observations | `{r} nrow(ert_df_clean)`  |
| Earliest year          | 1997                      |
| Latest year            | 2019                      |

### Graphical representation 
```{r}
ert_df_clean |>
  filter(row_regch_event != 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, fill = factor(row_regch_event))) +
  geom_bar() + 
  scale_fill_discrete(labels = c("Shift to autocracy", "Shift to democracy")) +
  scale_fill_grey(start = 0.3, end = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Number of regime changes", fill = "Regime change")
```
This bar chart shows the number of regimes changes per year across all countries in the sample. The blue portion of the bars quantify the amount of changes from an autocracy to a democracy while the red portions show the amount of changes from a democracy to an autocracy. There is no particular noticeable pattern in the data.


# Merging all our datasets into one 
Now that we have analysed each dataset individually, we must merge them into one clean dataset in order to facilitate our econometric analysis in the next part of the project. 
Ideally, our final dataset contains one row per country-year with the number of protests/demonstrations in that country-year, the ERT data for that country-year (political regime, changes...), and whether the protests/demonstrations in that country/year were more violent or non-violent. 

This implies three key steps: 
1 - Deciding which datasets / variables are useful. 
2 - Matching the datasets in terms of time frame. 
3 - Matching the datasets in terms of country coverage. 

1- A conclusion we can make from the dataset analysis above is that the Mass Mobilization and ACLED datasets measure very similar things: the number of protests per country-year. Thus, a choice must be made between these two datat sets. 

```{r}
mass_mob_cy <- mass_mob |>
  summarise(
    n_protests = sum(protest == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(country, year)
  )
```

```{r}
number_of_countries_mmcy <- dplyr::n_distinct(mass_mob_cy$country)
minimum_mmcy <-  min(mass_mob_cy$year)
maximum_mmcy <-  max(mass_mob_cy$year)
```

|                        |  ACLED                    | Mass Mobilization             |
|------------------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Number of observations | `{r} nrow(acled_df)`      |`{r} nrow(mass_mob_cy)`        |
| Number of countries    | `{r} number_of_countries` |`{r} number_of_countries_mmcy` |
| Earliest year          | `{r} minimum`             |`{r} minimum_mmcy`             |
| Latest year            | `{r} maximum`             |`{r} maximum_mmcy`             |

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
mass_mob_cy |>
  group_by(year) |>
   summarise(countries_mmcy = n_distinct(country)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = `year`, y = `countries_mmcy`)) +
geom_col()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
acled_df |>
  filter(!is.na(YEAR), !is.na(COUNTRY)) |>
  group_by(YEAR) |>
   summarise(countries = n_distinct(COUNTRY))|>
         
ggplot(aes(x = `YEAR`, y = `countries`)) +
geom_col()
```
:::
:::::

Clearly, the **Mass Mobiilization** dataset covers more countries over a larger time frame. Further, when looking into the codebook of both datasets, it appears that **Mass Mobiilization** is considerably more precise in its definition of protests: 

- They are defined as a gathering of 50 or more people making a demand for the government.

- They must be aimed for the state or state policy. 

- It captures only national initiatives of protesting targeted at home policies. 

- It excludes protests for other motivations (eg. religious).

As opposed to the **ACLED** dataset, this gives us access to very precise and targeted data which perfectly fits our analysis objectives: whether  politically-motivated protests lead to actual political changes. 

Thus, our explanatory variable will be entirely based on the **Mass Mobilization** data. 

2 - To determine our period of analysis, we look at the dataset which starts the latest and the dataset which ends the earliest. In this way, we maje sure that we all our variables are available for the same period. The dataset which starts the latest is the ACLED dataset (acled_df) which begins in 1997. The dataset which finishes the earliest is NAVCO dataset (navco_df) which finishes in 2019. Thus our time frame of analysis is 1997-2019. 

3 - The same logic applies to the country coverage. Not all datasets have observations for the same countries. Thus, we must determine which countries are in all datasets, and figure out a way to make these rows correspond through a common country code.
